paras: The lynching of Aaron Dickey took place at Bluffton, Georgia, shortly before March 4, 1888, when a party of young men tied Dickey, a Black man, to a tree and whipped him until he died. The men acted on the suspicion that Dickey was intimate with a white woman, and a dispatch from Cuthbert that ran in papers from Connecticut to Nevada called the killing "the execution of popular vengeance."

According to the Cuthbert dispatch, a white woman "whose name is not given" had become intimate with Dickey, whom it described as "well known as a desperado." It had "for some time been suspected" that their relations were "of a criminal character," and a party of young men decided to watch the woman's house.

After seeing Dickey enter the house, the men waited until night, or until midnight in other versions, then broke in and, in the dispatch's words, "found the couple as suspected." Dickey resisted, but the men surrounded and bound him, took him to a tree, bared his back and tied him to it.

They lashed his back with stout twigs, or a whip in the shorter versions, until it bled, working in relays so that one tired "detail" was relieved by another. Dickey cursed and then pleaded for mercy, and the men told him he would not live to see daylight. They left as day began to break, and Dickey died from the beating.
None of the men was named, and no report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The first report found was a one-paragraph item among Georgia news briefs in the Savannah Morning News on March 4, which called the affair "a horrible tale of debauchery and crime" and said Dickey had been whipped "by the indignant people of the community." A fuller dispatch datelined Cuthbert appeared the next day in the Springfield Daily Republic in Ohio, under the headline "THRASHED TO DEATH" and the deck "Vigilantes Mete Out Terrible Punishment to a Colored Man," and in the Waterbury Evening Democrat as "They Whipped Him to Death."

The story kept circulating for about two weeks: the New York Sun reprinted it from the New Orleans Times-Democrat on March 11, and the Carson City Morning Appeal and the Alexandria Gazette ran it as "Whipped to Death" on March 14. The Monmouth Inquirer reduced it to a single line in a weekly news summary, naming the attackers as "young white men," and the Cambria Freeman reprinted it on March 16.

Every version presented the attackers' suspicion as established fact and labeled Dickey a "desperado," while describing the whipping itself as "shocking" and "terrible punishment" without naming or condemning those who carried it out. The papers' dateline for the Cuthbert dispatch moved from March 5 to March 8 and March 12 as it was reprinted, though the event itself preceded the first Savannah report.

reader.title: Lynching of Aaron Dickey
bases: A party of young men seized Aaron Dickey at a house at night, tied him to a tree and whipped him until he died, telling him he would not live to see daylight (A2, A3, A1).

Dickey died of a whipping given by a 'party of young men' who worked in relieving 'details' with no lawful authority (A2, A3, A1); the dispatch called it 'the execution of popular vengeance' for his suspected relations with a white woman (A2, A4).

The Savannah Morning News state brief (A1) and the differently worded Cuthbert wire dispatch (A2, A3) agree on the victim's name, the place, the whipping and his death; all later items reprint the dispatch (A5-A8).

accounts.label: Georgia state news brief
accounts.gist: Dickey was 'terribly whipped by the indignant people of the community' after a tale of 'debauchery and crime' with a white woman, and died from the whipping.

accounts.label: Cuthbert wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Young men watched the woman's house, broke in at night, bound Dickey, tied him to a tree and lashed him in relays, telling him he would not live to see daylight; they left at dawn and he died.
